title: USA Today Co. sues OpenAI for $250M+ over 19 newspapers' training content
subtitle: The Manhattan federal complaint seeks statutory damages up to $150,000 per work and an order blocking continued use of the plaintiffs' articles.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: USA Today Co. and 13 affiliated newspapers filed suit against OpenAI in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on October 8, 2026, seeking more than $250 million in damages. The case, USA Today Co. v. OpenAI Foundation, docket No. 1:26-cv-08892, covers content from 19 publications, including USA Today, the Tennessean, and the Detroit Free Press. The complaint alleges that OpenAI used the plaintiffs' articles to train the models behind ChatGPT without a license, and that ChatGPT reproduces or summarizes those articles in ways that substitute for visits to the original sites.

The dollar figure is built from statutory copyright damages rather than lost revenue. Per Forbes' reading of the complaint, plaintiffs are asking for up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement and up to $25,000 per instance of removed or altered copyright management information. The filing also seeks a permanent injunction blocking continued infringement, which is the harder ask: a court order limiting model training or deployment would set a precedent that reaches well past the plaintiffs' own archives.

This is the third wave of newspaper suits against OpenAI, after the New York Times action in late 2023 and the Seattle Times / Newsday complaint from September 2026. The pattern is now consistent: large regional and local chains filing in Manhattan, with similar statutory damage math and similar injunction language. OpenAI has settled or struck licensing deals with some publishers (Associated Press, News Corp, Axel Springer), but the holdouts have grown in number as newsroom traffic from AI-generated summaries continues to climb.

A takeaway for learners: pay attention to what the suits ask for, not just the headline damages. The $250 million number drives press coverage; the injunction request is what would actually change how AI models are trained. If you are studying AI policy, read the prayer for relief sections — that is where the operative constraints live.
